title: This Real-Life Sea Monster is Controlled by Joysticks - Nautilus
gist: The oarfish — a snakelike fish that can exceed 25 feet — likely inspired sea-serpent legends and is called the 'doomsday fish' in Japan as a supposed earthquake omen, though a 2019 study found no link; its hypnotic movement is now inspiring roboticists.

themes.theme: Oarfish as the sea serpent of legend

insights.claim: The oarfish, with blank eyes, a feathered crest and a snakelike body that can exceed 25 feet, closely resembles the horned serpents on ancient maritime maps, suggesting sailors' sea-serpent sightings may have been real oarfish.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.quote: Sailors spotting sea serpents might not have been telling tall tales.
insights.locator: Sailors spotting sea serpents might not

insights.claim: A 16-foot oarfish that washed up in Bermuda in 1860 was taken as a sea monster and illustrated in Harper's Weekly.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.locator: When a 16-foot long specimen washed up

insights.claim: In Japanese folklore oarfish are messengers from the sea god's palace and called the 'doomsday fish', with sightings seen as harbingers of earthquakes and tsunamis — but a 2019 study of newspaper reports found no link between sightings and disasters.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Folk disaster omens lack predictive value — relevant to how markets and the public react to non-signals around catastrophe risk.
insights.quote: a 2019 study of newspaper reports uncovered no link between the two
insights.locator: And it’s not just Western cultures

insights.claim: The oarfish's unique, hypnotic swimming movements are inspiring roboticists, with a real-life version controlled by joysticks.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Undulating-body locomotion is a niche biomimetic design area for underwater robotics.
insights.locator: This Real-Life Sea Monster is Controlled by Joysticks
